impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting judgment as a matter of law that Teva's headache patents claiming methods of treating headache using humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies were invalid for failure to satisfy the written-description and enablement requirements of 35 U.S.C. § 112.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's JMOL of invalidity of Teva's patents covering methods of using humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies to treat headaches. The jury had found willful infringement and no invalidity, but the district court overturned the verdict on written description and enablement grounds. This case has significant implications for the scope of patent protection available for biologic drug claims defined by function rather than structure.
impacts.positiveImplications: Strengthens patent protection for pharmaceutical and biologic innovators by affirming that claims to methods using humanized antibodies can satisfy written description and enablement requirements even when the specification discloses only one specific antibody, provided prior art methods for making others were known.
impacts.negativeImplications: Creates potential exposure for companies like Eli Lilly whose competing products (e.g., galcanezumab/Emgality) may fall within the scope of broader biologic method patents that survive validity challenges.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent holder's conditioning of patent licenses on exclusive purchases of unpatented products constitutes unlawful tying under the Sherman Act when the unpatented products have substantial non-infringing uses.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed a jury verdict finding that Ingevity engaged in unlawful tying by conditioning licenses to its fuel vapor canister patent on customers' agreements to exclusively purchase Ingevity's unpatented carbon honeycomb products. The court upheld the antitrust liability and damages award, finding sufficient evidence that the tied products had substantial non-infringing uses (air-intake systems) beyond the patent's scope.
impacts.positiveImplications: Protects competitors like BASF from anticompetitive patent licensing practices, ensuring that patent holders cannot leverage patent rights to foreclose competition in markets for unpatented goods with substantial non-infringing uses.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders who bundle patent licenses with product purchase requirements face significant antitrust exposure. Companies must carefully evaluate whether tied products have substantial non-infringing uses before conditioning licenses on exclusive purchasing arrangements.

impacts.caseName: Trustees of Columbia University v. Gen Digital Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to detecting anomalous program executions by comparing function calls in an emulator to a model are abstract under Alice step one, and whether damages based on foreign sales of infringing software are recoverable.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated a $185 million jury verdict for Columbia, holding that claims directed to detecting anomalous program executions through emulator-based comparison to behavioral models are abstract under Alice step one and require further step-two analysis on remand. The court also ruled that the district court erred in allowing damages based on Norton's foreign software sales, limiting the extraterritorial reach of patent damages.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides defendants with stronger grounds to challenge cybersecurity and software patents under § 101 eligibility. The foreign sales ruling limits patent damages exposure for companies with global software distribution models.
impacts.negativeImplications: University and corporate patent holders with software-related patents face heightened § 101 vulnerability. The ruling on foreign sales narrows the damages base available to patent holders suing companies that sell software internationally.

impacts.caseName: GoTV Streaming, LLC v. Netflix, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to a server that tailors content presentation specifications to a wireless device's capabilities are ineligible for patenting under 35 U.S.C. § 101.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that GoTV's patents claiming systems for tailoring streamed content specifications to wireless device capabilities are ineligible under § 101, reversing the district court's judgment in GoTV's favor after a jury had found infringement and awarded $2.5 million in damages. The court found the claims directed to the abstract idea of adapting content to device capabilities.
impacts.positiveImplications: Strengthens § 101 defenses for streaming and technology companies against patent assertions covering content adaptation and delivery methods, which are common targets for patent assertion entities.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders in the content delivery and adaptive streaming space face increased risk that their patents will be invalidated as abstract, reducing the value of patent portfolios in this technology area.

impacts.caseName: VLSI Technology LLC v. Intel Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting summary judgment of noninfringement of a multicore processor patent on extraterritoriality grounds and in striking a patent holder's damages expert theories.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed-in-part the district court's grant of summary judgment of noninfringement to Intel on the extraterritoriality ground, finding genuine issues of material fact regarding where the patented method was performed. The court affirmed on other grounds and remanded for further proceedings. This case addresses the territorial limits of U.S. patent law for semiconductor and processor technology.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders asserting processor and semiconductor patents gain clarity that extraterritoriality defenses may not be resolved on summary judgment when there are factual disputes about where methods are performed.
impacts.negativeImplications: Semiconductor companies like Intel face continued exposure to patent infringement claims even where substantial design and manufacturing activities occur abroad, as the location of method performance remains a fact-intensive inquiry.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the ITC correctly found that Apple's importation and sale of Apple Watch models with blood oxygen measurement functionality violated § 337 of the Tariff Act by infringing Masimo's patents.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the ITC's finding that Apple violated § 337 by importing Apple Watches incorporating blood oxygen sensing technology covered by Masimo's patents, upholding the limited exclusion order barring importation of infringing devices. The court found no error in the domestic industry determination, validity rulings, or infringement findings.
impacts.positiveImplications: Strengthens the ability of medical technology patent holders to use ITC exclusion orders to block importation of consumer electronics incorporating patented health-monitoring features.
impacts.negativeImplications: Major consumer electronics companies face significant market disruption from ITC exclusion orders when incorporating patented health and medical sensor technologies into their products, potentially requiring product redesigns or licensing.

impacts.caseName: Global Tubing LLC v. Tenaris Coiled Tubes LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether summary judgment was properly granted on inequitable conduct and Walker Process fraud claims relating to patents obtained after acquisition of prior art materials describing similar technology.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated summary judgments on both inequitable conduct (granted for Global Tubing) and Walker Process antitrust fraud (granted for Tenaris), finding genuine disputes of material fact on both issues. The case involves allegations that Tenaris failed to disclose prior art CYMAX documents to the PTO when prosecuting patents for its BlueCoil coiled tubing product, raising questions of both patent enforceability and antitrust attempted monopolization.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies defending against patent assertions gain renewed ability to pursue both inequitable conduct defenses and Walker Process antitrust counterclaims where a patent applicant may have withheld material prior art acquired through corporate acquisitions.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that obtain patents after acquiring businesses with related prior art face significant litigation risk on both inequitable conduct and antitrust grounds if they fail to adequately disclose acquired prior art during patent prosecution.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a Rule 30(b)(6) corporate representative may testify beyond personal knowledge for summary judgment purposes and whether the on-sale bar under 35 U.S.C. § 102(b) requires that a prior sale expressly disclose the functionality of the prior art device.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of invalidity under the pre-AIA on-sale bar, holding that 30(b)(6) corporate representative testimony is admissible at summary judgment even when the witness lacks personal knowledge of the facts, and that the on-sale bar does not require prior art sales to expressly disclose device functionality. The court also ruled that computer source code, as commands rather than assertions, is not hearsay.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants challenging patent validity gain powerful evidentiary tools: 30(b)(6) testimony from corporate successors is admissible to prove historical sales, and source code is non-hearsay evidence of device functionality for on-sale bar purposes.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face broader invalidity exposure as the on-sale bar can be proven through corporate representative testimony without personal knowledge of historical sales and through source code analysis of prior art products, even when original engineers are unavailable.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to non-uniform constellations for digital communication systems are eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and how eligibility analysis applies when patented technology is incorporated into industry standards.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit partially vacated and partially affirmed summary judgment of patent eligibility for claims related to non-uniform constellation designs used in digital communication standards. The court vacated eligibility for certain claims of two patents while affirming eligibility for claims of two other patents, and affirmed infringement and damages findings. This case is significant for standard-essential patent holders in telecommunications.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders with claims tied to specific technical implementations in industry standards (rather than abstract mathematical concepts) may survive § 101 challenges, preserving the ability to enforce standard-essential patents.
impacts.negativeImplications: Electronics manufacturers implementing communication standards face ongoing patent infringement risk, and the split eligibility ruling creates uncertainty about which types of signal processing claims survive § 101 scrutiny.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the PTAB correctly construed claims in a patent related to streaming partly encrypted media content, and whether the Board's claim construction affected its obviousness analysis.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the PTAB's claim construction of DivX's patent covering systems for streaming partly encrypted media content and vacated the Board's decision rejecting Netflix's obviousness challenge. The court adopted a different construction of the disputed claim term and remanded for further proceedings, impacting the validity of patents in the streaming media encryption space.
impacts.positiveImplications: Streaming and content delivery companies benefit from the reversal, as it reopens the possibility that prior art renders encryption-related streaming patents obvious, potentially reducing licensing costs.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders in the streaming media and DRM space face renewed validity challenges following the court's adoption of broader claim constructions that may expose more claims to prior art.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court abused its discretion in excluding a patent holder's damages expert report and granting summary judgment based on absence of a remedy.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's exclusion of Exafer's damages expert report in a patent case against Microsoft's Azure platform and vacated the resulting summary judgment for Microsoft based on absence of a remedy. The court held that the district court applied too strict a standard in evaluating the reliability of the damages methodology.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders gain broader latitude in presenting damages evidence, as courts must not apply overly stringent Daubert standards that effectively bar patent damages claims at the expert-exclusion stage.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies like Microsoft face increased patent litigation costs as more damages theories survive Daubert challenges, making it harder to obtain early dispositive rulings in patent cases.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the PTO Director's instructions to the PTAB governing discretionary denial of inter partes review institution constitute 'general statements of policy' exempt from APA notice-and-comment rulemaking requirements.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that the PTO Director's instructions governing discretionary IPR non-institution decisions are general statements of policy exempt from notice-and-comment rulemaking under the APA. The court reasoned that the instructions do not bind the Director, who retains ultimate authority over institution decisions, and that non-institution is statutorily insulated from judicial review.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders benefit from the PTO retaining broad discretion to deny IPR petitions without being constrained by formal rulemaking, preserving flexibility in the patent review system.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies and other frequent IPR petitioners face continued uncertainty and limited recourse when IPR petitions are denied under discretionary frameworks that need not undergo public notice-and-comment procedures.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly approved a $125 million class action settlement of claims that the federal judiciary overcharged PACER users, and whether incentive awards to class representative nonprofit organizations were permissible.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's approval of a $125 million settlement in a nationwide class action claiming the federal judiciary exceeded its statutory authority by using PACER fees to fund non-PACER expenses. The court upheld the settlement, attorneys' fee awards, and incentive awards to the three nonprofit class representatives, finding no abuse of discretion.
impacts.positiveImplications: The settlement provides substantial reimbursement to hundreds of thousands of PACER users, including businesses and law firms that regularly access federal court records, and validates the use of class actions to challenge excessive government fees.

impacts.caseName: Ascendis Pharma A/S v. BioMarin Pharmaceutical Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an ITC respondent may obtain a mandatory stay of a refiled district court declaratory judgment action under 28 U.S.C. § 1659(a)(2) when it previously filed a declaratory judgment action and missed the deadline for seeking a stay.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that an ITC respondent cannot circumvent the mandatory stay deadline under § 1659(a)(2) by dismissing and refiling a declaratory judgment action to obtain a new 30-day window. The court ruled that BioMarin could not use this procedural maneuver to stay Ascendis's district court action challenging a pharmaceutical patent while the ITC investigation was pending.
impacts.positiveImplications: Pharmaceutical and technology companies bringing declaratory judgment actions are protected from opponents gaming the mandatory stay provisions by dismissing and refiling cases to reset filing deadlines.
impacts.negativeImplications: ITC respondents who miss the § 1659(a)(2) deadline cannot cure the deficiency through refiling, potentially forcing them to litigate on parallel fronts in both the ITC and district court.

impacts.caseName: International Medical Devices, Inc. v. Cornell
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the jury had a legally sufficient evidentiary basis to find that asserted trade secrets were protectable under California law when the information was allegedly generally known in the field.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the denial of JMOL on trade secret misappropriation claims involving cosmetic penile implant technology, finding insufficient evidence that the asserted trade secrets were actually protectable because the underlying information was generally known. The court vacated the reasonable royalty award, exemplary damages, and permanent injunction, while affirming the counterfeiting claim and damages for unauthorized use of the Penuma® mark.
impacts.positiveImplications: Businesses defending trade secret claims benefit from heightened scrutiny of whether asserted secrets are truly not generally known, providing stronger JMOL grounds where the plaintiff fails to differentiate claimed secrets from publicly available information.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies relying on trade secret protection must ensure robust evidence that their claimed secrets are not generally known in the industry, as courts will scrutinize the evidentiary basis for trade secret protectability even after a favorable jury verdict.
